title: The Bishop of Digne
text: In 1815 the little town of Digne, in the mountains of the south of France, has had for nine years a bishop unlike any other. Monseigneur Myriel is seventy-five, and the poor call him Monseigneur Bienvenu, “Welcome.” Three days after arriving he gave his palace to the hospital and moved into its cramped house; he gives away nearly all his income, tours his diocese on foot or on a donkey, and once crossed bandit country alone to reach a village of shepherds. He lives with his gentle sister, Mademoiselle Baptistine, and their bustling servant, Madame Magloire, who have both learned to live by his fearless ways.

Hugo spends these chapters showing what the Bishop is rather than telling a story about him: his mild wit, his indulgence toward the weak, the day he spent beside a condemned man on the scaffold, and his visit to a dying old revolutionary shunned by the whole town, which ends with the Bishop on his knees asking the old man’s blessing. His one fault, the narrator says, was a royalist coldness toward Napoleon in his fall.
As chapter 14 closes, nothing has yet happened to this good man. He keeps only two luxuries, six silver forks and spoons and a pair of silver candlesticks, and his front door has no lock.

title: The convict and the candlesticks
text: In Digne in 1815 lives Monseigneur Myriel, a saintly old bishop whom the poor call Bienvenu, “Welcome.” He has given his palace to the sick and his income to the poor, and he never locks his door. His only luxuries are some silver tableware and two silver candlesticks.

One October evening a ragged, exhausted traveller is turned away from every inn and door in town, even a dog’s kennel. At the Bishop’s house he announces the worst at once: he is Jean Valjean, a convict just released after nineteen years in the galleys of Toulon, carrying the yellow passport that marks him everywhere. The Bishop sets another place with the silver and gives him a bed. Hugo then tells his story. A tree-pruner who stole a loaf for his sister’s seven starving children, he got five years and, after four escape attempts, served nineteen, and the galleys turned him into a man who hates society and God.

In the night Valjean steals the silver and flees over the garden wall. When gendarmes drag him back, the Bishop says he gave it to him, hands him the candlesticks as well, and tells him that he has bought his soul for God and that he has promised to use the silver to become an honest man.

Valjean wanders the fields in turmoil and, almost without thinking, puts his foot on a coin dropped by a little Savoyard chimney-sweep, Petit-Gervais, and drives the boy away. Then, horrified at himself, he searches in vain for the child and weeps for the first time in nineteen years. As chapter 27 closes, a man has been seen that night kneeling in prayer at the Bishop’s door, and Valjean is changed, though the narrator does not yet say into what.

title: Fantine’s summer
text: In Digne in 1815 the saintly Bishop Myriel took in Jean Valjean, a convict released after nineteen years in the galleys for stealing a loaf. Valjean robbed him of his silver in the night; when the gendarmes brought him back, the Bishop said it was a gift, added his two silver candlesticks, and told him he had bought his soul for God. Shaken, Valjean then robbed a little chimney-sweep, Petit-Gervais, of a coin, and wept with remorse when the boy was gone.

Hugo leaves him there and jumps to Paris in 1817. Four students, led by the rich, witty Félix Tholomyès, spend a bright summer Sunday at Saint-Cloud with their four young working-girl mistresses. Among the girls is Fantine, a foundling from Montreuil-sur-Mer, beautiful and modest, for whom Tholomyès is a first and only love. All day the men promise the girls a “surprise.”

After dinner at Bombarda’s the men kiss the girls and slip out. The surprise is a letter: they have taken the coach home to their families and respectability, and the affair is over. The other girls laugh it off. As chapter 36 closes, Fantine laughs too, then weeps alone, for she has a little child by Tholomyès.

title: The Lark of Montfermeil
text: In 1815 the Bishop of Digne answered the theft of his silver by the released convict Jean Valjean with a gift of his candlesticks, telling him he had bought his soul for God. Valjean, after robbing a little chimney-sweep of a coin, wept with remorse; the narrator has said no more of him since.

In Paris in 1817 Fantine, a young working girl, was abandoned by her lover, the student Tholomyès, who went home to his family and left her with their small daughter, Cosette. Ten months later, with no money and no work, she walks out of Paris toward her native town of Montreuil-sur-Mer. At Montfermeil she passes an inn where two happy little girls are swinging, and she leaves Cosette with their mother, Madame Thénardier, paying in advance and promising monthly payments.

The Thénardiers are a nasty pair: she is a coarse brute who loves only her own daughters, Éponine and Azelma; he is a scheming innkeeper who boasts of having been a sergeant at Waterloo. They pawn Cosette’s clothes, dress her in rags, feed her under the table with the dog and cat, and keep inventing reasons to raise the price. As chapter 39 closes, Cosette is about five, the household drudge, beaten by Madame Thénardier and scorned by the girls, and the village calls her the Lark. Her mother, far away, keeps paying.

title: The mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer
text: In 1815 the Bishop of Digne forgave the released convict Jean Valjean for stealing his silver and gave him the candlesticks too; Valjean, after robbing a little chimney-sweep, wept with remorse and vanished from the story. In 1817 the young Fantine was abandoned in Paris by her lover Tholomyès and left their daughter, Cosette, with the Thénardiers, innkeepers at Montfermeil, who make the child their drudge and keep raising what they charge her mother.

Fantine has gone home to Montreuil-sur-Mer and found it transformed. In December 1815 a stranger arrived with a knapsack and a stick, saved two children from a fire, and revolutionised the local trade in black glass trinkets. Father Madeleine, as everyone calls him, has built a great factory that employs anyone willing to be honest, poured his profits into schools and hospital beds, and in 1820 was made mayor. He is quiet, solitary and enormously strong; when the papers report the death of the Bishop of Digne, he goes into mourning and says he served in the family in his youth. Only one man distrusts him: Javert, a police inspector born in a prison, who worships authority and despises anyone who has ever broken the law. When old Fauchelevent, a carter who dislikes the mayor, is pinned under his cart, Javert remarks that he has known only one man strong enough to lift it, a convict at Toulon. Madeleine crawls under and lifts it, then finds Fauchelevent a post as gardener at a convent in Paris.

Fantine worked in the mayor’s factory until a gossip discovered her child and the forewoman dismissed her in his name, without his knowing. Lying letters from the Thénardiers drove her to sell her hair, then her front teeth, then herself. Hating the mayor she blames for her ruin, she becomes a prostitute.

One snowy night a dandy named Bamatabois stuffs snow down her back; she claws him, and Javert sentences her to six months in prison. Madeleine walks in, orders her released, and, when she spits in his face, overrules the furious Javert and promises her that her debts will be paid and her child brought to her. As chapter 52 closes, Fantine has fainted kissing his hand, and Javert has been humiliated in front of a prostitute.

title: The Champmathieu affair
text: In 1815 the Bishop of Digne forgave the released convict Jean Valjean for stealing his silver, gave him his candlesticks too, and told him he had bought his soul for God; Valjean robbed a little Savoyard, Petit-Gervais, of a coin, then wept with remorse. In 1817 Fantine, abandoned by her lover, left her daughter Cosette with the Thénardiers at Montfermeil, who mistreat the child and bleed her mother for money. At Montreuil-sur-Mer the good mayor, Father Madeleine, rescued Fantine, ruined and sick, from Inspector Javert.

Madeleine nurses Fantine and sends the Thénardiers money to bring Cosette, but Thénardier, smelling profit, invents bills and keeps the child, and Fantine is dying of a chest disease. Then Javert comes to ask to be dismissed. In his anger he denounced the mayor to Paris as the escaped convict Jean Valjean, and he was wrong: the real Jean Valjean has been found, an old apple-thief called Champmathieu whom three former convicts have recognised. He goes on trial at Arras tomorrow and faces the galleys for life.

Now the narrator says plainly what the reader may have guessed: M. Madeleine is Jean Valjean. Through a night of torment he argues both ways, to stay silent and go on doing good for a whole town and for Fantine and her child, or to give himself up and keep his soul. He burns his convict’s clothes and the coin he took from Petit-Gervais, and drives to Arras through a chain of breakdowns that seem to beg him to turn back.

In the courtroom he sees a bewildered old man who looks like himself as he entered Digne, condemned by everyone’s certainty. He stands up, tells the court that he is Jean Valjean, proves it with details only the three convicts could know, and walks out with no one daring to stop him. As chapter 65 closes, Champmathieu has been freed, and the mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer has named himself a convict before the whole court, while Fantine still waits for her child.

title: Fantine dies, Valjean flees
text: Jean Valjean, a convict whom the Bishop of Digne answered with mercy in 1815, remade himself as M. Madeleine, the beloved manufacturer and mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer. He took in Fantine, a ruined, dying young mother whose daughter, Cosette, is a drudge at the Thénardiers’ inn at Montfermeil, and promised to bring her the child. Then, to save an innocent old man, Champmathieu, from the galleys in his place, he declared himself Jean Valjean in open court at Arras.

He comes back at dawn with his hair turned white and goes straight to Fantine, whose first word is “Cosette?” Then Javert appears in the doorway with a warrant, seizes him by the collar, and shouts that there is no mayor, only the convict Jean Valjean. Fantine, learning that her child was never brought, dies of the shock. Valjean lays out her body, whispers something in her ear, and gives himself up.

That night he breaks out of the town jail, slips back to his room, wraps up the Bishop’s candlesticks and leaves money for the poor. When Javert bursts in, Sister Simplice, the nun who has never told a lie, tells him two and saves Valjean. The town turns against its former mayor, its prosperity begins to fail, and Fantine is buried in a common grave.
As chapter 70 closes, Valjean has vanished toward Paris with Javert on his trail, and Cosette is still at Montfermeil, her mother dead and the man who meant to fetch her a hunted fugitive.

title: The field of Waterloo
text: Jean Valjean, a convict whom the Bishop of Digne answered with mercy, became M. Madeleine, the good mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer, until he gave himself up in court to save an innocent man who had been taken for him. Inspector Javert arrested him at the bedside of Fantine, the ruined young mother he had promised to reunite with her daughter, and she died of the shock. Valjean broke out of jail and fled toward Paris. Cosette, Fantine’s child, remains a drudge at the Thénardiers’ inn at Montfermeil.

Volume II opens with a long detour. In 1861 the narrator walks onto the battlefield of Waterloo and retells the battle of 18 June 1815: the rain that delayed Napoleon’s guns, the hidden hollow road of Ohain that swallowed the French cuirassiers, the late arrival of the Prussians, the death of the Imperial Guard, and Cambronne’s defiant word. Hugo reads the day as chance and Providence rather than genius, and Waterloo as the victory of the old monarchies over the Revolution, ushering in the Restoration of the Bourbons.

Then he returns to the field by moonlight, where marauders strip the dead. One prowler, with a sutler’s cart nearby, robs a buried cavalry officer of his ring, cross, watch and purse, and in doing so drags him alive from under the corpses in the hollow road. The officer, believing himself rescued, asks his name: Thénardier. His own is Pontmercy. As chapter 89 closes, the reader knows what kind of “sergeant at Waterloo” the Montfermeil innkeeper was, and an officer named Pontmercy believes he owes him his life.
